title: Optimal approximation of general-domain k-CSP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
context:
Open Problem 3 says the factor is known optimal when \(d=\Omega(k)\). The same chapter’s introduction and the cited 2014 primary paper instead establish matching bounds when \(k\ge d\). The 2016 paper’s Figure 1 independently confirms the latter regime. This review follows those explicit theorem statements and does not repeat the reversed inequality as a fact.

The 2016 paper gives an \(\Omega(\log d/d^{k-1})\) approximation and, assuming UGC, hardness at factor \(2^{O(k\log k)}(\log d)^{k/2}/d^{k-1}\) for each \(k\ge2\) and sufficiently large \(d\). Together with the arity-sensitive algorithm this explains the source’s scale involving the maximum of \(k\) and \(\log d\). The displayed hardness need not match it to a universal constant.

Bakshi’s August 2026 preprint claims, for every fixed \(k\ge10\) and accuracy parameter \(\varepsilon>0\), an expected ratio \(k/2^{k}-\varepsilon\). The theorem includes the finite-precision loss even though the abstract emphasizes the ideal ratio. The domain is fixed to two values.

Makarychev’s contemporaneous note independently claims a \((1-o_{k}(1))k/2^{k}\) guarantee and explicitly connects it to the Boolean conjecture. These preprints concern Open Problem 2 of the survey; neither gives the requested matching dependence on an arbitrary growing domain size. Their proofs were not independently verified in this review.
why: The question asks how arity and the number of labels jointly control the best efficient approximation of arbitrary local constraints. Matching bounds would explain the transition between Boolean-like behavior and large-domain instances, with consequences for the quantitative strength of probabilistically checkable proofs.
status_note: Read the complete survey problem and its introductory comparison, the 2014 primary theorem paper, and the 2016 algorithm/hardness statements and model definitions. Read the scope and principal claims of both August 2026 Boolean preprints. The source’s known-regime typo is corrected, but its intended hardness assumption and full uniformity convention are not uniquely recovered. This card remains needs_specification; no new preprint is treated as a verified general-domain resolution.
review_note: The quantitative approximation scale is recovered, but the source does not select one hardness assumption or one uniformity convention for its optimality claim. Specify whether matching lower bounds should be ordinary NP-hardness, UGC-hardness or an actual algorithmic impossibility under a stated separation, and whether algorithms may depend on fixed arity/domain or must be uniform in both. Randomized expected guarantees also require an appropriate assumption when converted from hardness to impossibility. Do not treat the source’s reversed parameter inequality as the intended regime.

progress.text: The arity-sensitive algorithm matches known hardness when arity is at least the domain size.
The logarithmic-domain approximation and near-matching UGC-hardness improve the large-domain regime.
The survey asks whether the combined approximation scale is optimal across the full parameter range.
Two preprints claim improvements to the leading constant for the Boolean case; they do not resolve the general-domain question.

definitions:
An unweighted instance has explicitly listed variables \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) taking values in \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\), and a finite list of constraints. Each constraint names at most \(k\) distinct variables and gives the truth table of a predicate on their values. Repeated constraints count separately. A feasible output assigns one domain value to every variable. Its value \(\operatorname{val}_{I}(a)\) is the number of satisfied constraints; \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the maximum of that value over all assignments. This is maximization, not deciding whether all constraints can be simultaneously satisfied.

The ordinary explicit representation includes variable indices, the domain description, constraint scopes and all predicate tables. Polynomial time must be measured in its full bit length \(L\). Succinct circuits for predicates would be a different representation. The source and cited papers also use nonnegative weighted constraints in intermediate formulations; the displayed task is the usual unweighted problem.

An expected randomized approximation guarantee \(\rho\in[0,1]\) means
\[
\mathbb E[\operatorname{val}_{I}(A(I))]\ge \rho\,\operatorname{OPT}(I)
\]
for every fixed instance, where expectation is over the algorithm’s random bits. A deterministic guarantee requires the inequality for its single output. The condition is automatic when the optimum is zero. Maximizing the fraction of constraints satisfied gives the same multiplicative comparison to the optimum fraction.

For an illustration of a precise algorithmic quantity, one can fix \(k,d\) and define \(\alpha(k,d)\) as the supremum of such expected ratios attained by uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines on all instances with these fixed parameters. In this convention the algorithm and its polynomial running-time exponent may depend on \(k,d\). A simultaneous bound \(\alpha(k,d)=\Theta(q(k,d))\) would require constants independent of both parameters. Requiring one algorithm polynomial in \(L\) when \(k,d\) are variable inputs is a distinct convention. The source’s short open question does not explicitly choose between them.

A hardness theorem is another kind of statement. NP-hardness of a gap means there is a polynomial-time reduction from every NP decision problem to distinguishing instances whose optimum is above a specified completeness threshold from those below a soundness threshold. It becomes a deterministic algorithmic impossibility only with a separation assumption such as \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). UGC-hardness additionally assumes the Unique Games Conjecture: for every sufficiently small positive \(\eta,\gamma\), some fixed finite alphabet makes it NP-hard to distinguish permutation-constraint games with optimum fraction at least \(1-\eta\) from those with optimum at most \(\gamma\). A permutation constraint between two variables requires their labels to correspond under a specified bijection.

Neither ordinary NP-hardness nor UGC plus \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone automatically excludes bounded-error randomized algorithms. For that interpretation an appropriate randomized complexity separation must also be stated. Thus “optimal” cannot silently mean all these formulations at once.
answer_criterion: After fixing the hardness assumption and algorithmic uniformity convention, establish matching approximation and hardness bounds up to constants independent of arity and domain size, or prove that the proposed scale fails in some asymptotic regime. A sharp Boolean leading constant, a result only when arity is at least the domain size, or an extra unbounded logarithmic loss does not settle the general-domain question. The unresolved specification choices must be fixed before this is a complete benchmark.
